title: A Verdict for the Letter
premise: Kestrel Eastwick, concierge at the Gullwing Hotel, has built her life on noticing without being noticed — until a gaunt stranger named Ivo Marsh pays a year's lodging in advance and asks her to prove that his sister, drowned thirty years ago in the tidal caves below Saltmere, was murdered before it can happen again. As Kestrel files away alibis, letters, and lies from the town's founding families, she discovers the 'murder' Ivo fears is a ritual reenactment performed every three decades by those who survived the original night and owe their fortunes to it. The tide will give up what it took only once: when Kestrel finally reads the letter hidden in the hotel's ledgers — written by her own mother, the original intended victim who escaped — she must choose between exposing the town's inheritance of guilt and protecting the one person left alive who still benefits. In the end, the ceremony is interrupted, the last conspirator confesses on the cave steps as the water rises, and Kestrel trades her invisibility for the truth, becoming the town's witness instead of its keeper.
about_author: Rosalind Coldharbour spent a decade working front desks in coastal hotels before turning to crime fiction, collecting the small cruelties guests assume staff won't remember. She writes from a rented room above a shuttered seaside arcade, where the tide is audible at all hours.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A stranger named Ivo Marsh checks into the Gullwing, pays twelve months upfront, and asks her to prove a murder hasn't happened yet. Kestrel's instinct is to deflect; instead she takes the money and the file. Beat: curiosity overriding self-preservation.

chapters.title: The Alphabet of Small Sins
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. We see her private ledger system — decades of guest confessions filed A to Z — and realize Ivo's name triggers an old entry: his sister Verity, 1994. Beat: the past knocking on a very organized door.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. He walks the shingle below the tidal caves, remembering the night he was pulled from the water at nine years old while Verity wasn't. He knows more than he told Kestrel. Beat: grief disguised as investigation.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She interviews the four surviving heirs of Saltmere's great houses — the Vances, the Merricks, old Mrs. Pell, and Judge Halloway — all of whom were teenagers in 1994. Each alibi is polished, rehearsed, identical in structure. Beat: too-perfect answers smell like rot.

chapters.title: Room 12 Never Slept
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Hotel records show Room 12 was booked every July for thirty years under rotating aliases — always the same handwriting. Kestrel recognizes it with a chill she can't place. Beat: the first crack in her own memory.

chapters.title: A Rehearsal for Drowning
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. He finds chalk marks and a wax-sealed envelope in the cave mouth: instructions dated for this July, listing five names — four heirs and one blank line. Beat: dread crystallizing into certainty.

chapters.title: The Concierge Who Saw Nothing
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell's POV. The elderly matriarch recalls 1994 obliquely, through etiquette and euphemism, revealing that six children entered the caves that night and only five came out — and that the sixth was a hotel maid's daughter. Beat: sympathy curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: Ledger Entries, Mother's Hand
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Comparing the Room 12 handwriting to her late mother's effects, Kestrel finds the match: her mother was the maid, and the sixth child was Kestrel herself, age four. Beat: the investigator becomes the subject.

chapters.title: Alibis Woven Thirty Years Ago
chapters.summary: Judge Halloway's POV. He reconstructs the official story — accidental drowning, closed verdict — and we watch him stitch it in real time, showing how a lie is maintained across decades. Beat: institutional evil, calmly administered.

chapters.title: The Blank Line
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Deciphering the cave envelope, she realizes the fifth name was never filled because the ritual requires the maid's daughter — her — to return willingly. Ivo knew all along. Betrayal scene. Beat: trust inverted.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Low Water
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Ivo, alternating. She demands the truth; he admits he chose her because only she can open the sealed family archive, keyed to Eastwick blood. Their alliance fractures and reforms on harder terms. Beat: reluctant partnership.

chapters.title: What Verity Knew
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. A recovered diary shows Verity discovered the heirs' smuggling operation the night she died — she wasn't sacrificed to the sea but silenced by it. Beat: the mystery's engine revealed.

chapters.title: The Vance Confession (Unrecorded)
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Young Edmund Vance, drunk and terrified, half-confesses in the hotel bar; Kestrel records nothing, filing it instead — until she realizes he'll be dead by morning if she waits. Beat: the price of professional detachment.

chapters.title: Edmund's Quiet Exit
chapters.summary: Mrs. Pell's POV. Edmund is found 'gone abroad,' his house scrubbed, his dog rehomed. The town accepts it instantly. Kestrel does not. Beat: horror of a community fluent in looking away.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Wall
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following her mother's ledger marginalia, Kestrel opens a cavity behind the front desk and finds the letter: her mother's full account of 1994, naming everyone, written the week before her own convenient death. Beat: grief and fury fused.

chapters.title: Rising Water, Rising Stakes
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The equinoctial tide approaches; the heirs accelerate preparations, and Judge Halloway serves Kestrel with an eviction notice backdated with elegant legality. Beat: the machinery closing in.

chapters.title: An Offer of Silence
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Mrs. Pell offers Kestrel the hotel itself — inheritance, belonging, everything she's never had — in exchange for the letter and her silence. Kestrel almost says yes. Beat: temptation made genuinely reasonable.

chapters.title: The Night of the Ceremony
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The four heirs descend to the caves with candles and a chair; Ivo goes as bait; Kestrel goes as the fifth name, voluntarily. Beat: terror chosen freely.

chapters.title: Verdict Below the Waterline
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In the cave, Kestrel reads her mother's letter aloud by candlelight, forcing each heir to hear their own words read back. Halloway orders the others to seal the entrance. Beat: climax — testimony versus tide.

chapters.title: What the Tide Gives Up
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The spring tide floods the lower chamber; in the chaos, Verity's remains surface exactly where the diary said they would, undeniable, physical evidence. Halloway breaks. Beat: the sea testifies.

chapters.title: Filed Under E for Eastwick
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Aftermath: arrests, the hotel sold to pay restitution, Kestrel keeping only the ledger and the letter. She begins a new file labeled with names, not sins. Beat: mourning the invisibility she chose.

chapters.title: A Witness Stays On
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, epilogue tone. Months later, Kestrel runs a modest guesthouse and teaches herself to be seen; Ivo visits each July, and together they walk the shingle at low water, no longer afraid of what it returns. Final beat: survival's price paid, memory inherited honestly.
